title: New Grub Street: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to New Grub Street Unpacked, a close reading of George Gissing's 1891 novel about the London literary world — its ambitions, its failures, and its machinery.
Gissing wrote a book about writers trying to survive — and in doing so produced one of the most unsparing portraits of the literary marketplace ever committed to paper.
Over the course of this episode, we'll be reading it closely — very closely — with three remarkable guests.

Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, a writer, and the voice behind more classic novel audiobooks than anyone alive — he comes to Gissing as a performer, listening for the rhythms, the timing, the moments that only come alive when spoken.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been asking what moral imagination looks like in fiction — he reads novels as stories about individual character tested by circumstance, and he is not always kind about what he finds.

And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he is interested in what institutions do to people, and he has a great deal to say about what Gissing's London does to its writers.
Oliver — before we started recording you said something that's stayed with me: that this novel needs to be heard to be understood.
Reardon's great speech about the successful novelists — on the page it can look like a bloke having a moan.
Can you read it to us, and make the case for why it's something more than that?
Oh, it is absolutely a moan — that's precisely what makes it magnificent.
Gissing gives Reardon the register of a man who has rehearsed this speech in his own head many times — and that's what you have to bring out when you read it.
There's a drumbeat to it — listen.
"They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school men, University men, club men, society men."
Do you hear that? Four nouns, each one a little world — public-school, University, club, society.
It's a litany. Gissing is writing for the voice here — the repetition is the argument.
Reardon isn't explaining his contempt — he's performing it, and the performance is the only power he has left.
Oliver is right that there's a performance — but I want to press on what that performance is doing ideologically.
Because Reardon isn't just venting — he's performing a precise social cartography.
Those four nouns describe a complete infrastructure of privilege — the school, the degree, the club, the social network.
He can name the machine perfectly, even as it destroys him. That's the tragedy — and the sharpness.
And the setting in which this speech is delivered matters enormously — Gissing puts us in this extraordinary room beforehand.
Let me read you what the penny reading-room writing chamber actually looks like:

"The walls of this last retreat were of blue plaster and sloped inwards from the floor; along them stood school desks with benches, and in one place was suspended a ragged and dirty card announcing that paper and envelopes could be purchased downstairs."
That is not a stage set. That is a mechanism — designed to extract just enough intellectual labour from just enough desperate people to make a profit.
Daniel, I appreciate the vigour — but I think you're asking the room to carry more freight than Gissing intends.
It is simply a room. A rather depressing room, yes — blue sloped walls, school desks, an enormous basket of waste paper.
Gissing is a superb naturalist — he puts his characters somewhere real, and then watches what they do.
What interests me is not the room — it is what Reardon does with his mind inside it.
Because that speech, which Oliver has read with such splendid energy — I hear something else in it.
I hear envy dressed up as justice. The rancour Reardon claims to have transcended is the very thing consuming him.
He says it would be — and I am quoting now — 'small-minded to think of them with rancour.'
"It would be small-minded to think of them with rancour, but, by Apollo! I know that we should change places with them if the work we have done were justly weighed against theirs."
'By Apollo.' The classical invocation is meant to dignify the claim — but it only exposes the self-dramatisation.
Gissing is too honest a novelist to let that pass without irony.
Edmund, I won't quarrel with the irony — Gissing absolutely puts it there.
But I'd say the self-dramatisation is the point, not the flaw. Reardon is a writer — self-dramatisation is his only remaining instrument.
And when he performs his bitterness — when he calls on Apollo in a blue-walled garret — Gissing is giving us something that is simultaneously ridiculous and completely heartbreaking.
That double effect is very hard to write. Gissing is working at the top of his talent there.
Daniel, I want to put something to you directly.
You say the system requires Reardon's failure — it is structurally produced.
Edmund says the failure is a failure of moral imagination — self-pity dressed as analysis.
You're both claiming Gissing as the unsentimental novelist. How are those two things not the same argument?
They sound the same — but the difference is everything, and it's a difference of where you locate causation.
Edmund's reading places the moral failure inside Reardon — it is his weakness of will, his corrosive envy, that does for him.
My reading says: look at where he is sitting when he makes that speech.
He is in a room with sloped walls and school desks, surrounded by ink blotches and waste paper — the physical detritus of failed literary ambition.
The system has put him there. His envy is the system's product — not a pre-existing character flaw.
Gissing is unsentimental about individuals, yes — but he is also showing us the conditions that make individual virtue nearly impossible.
That is a seductive argument — and I find myself partially persuaded by it, which is unusual and faintly alarming.
But I would say this: Gissing gives us other characters in comparable poverty who do not corrode.
Biffen is in that same room, eating the same squalid feast — and Biffen is not consumed by rancour in the same way.
The conditions are constant. The character varies. That is Gissing insisting on the reality of individual moral life.
Edmund's Biffen point is genuinely good — I'll concede that immediately.
But then that's the thing about performing your bitterness — it's not the same as feeling it more acutely than someone else.
Reardon is a novelist. He aestheticises his suffering — he can't help it.
Does that make him more sympathetic or less? Honestly — I've been reading this book for twenty years and I still can't tell you.
And I think that sustained ambiguity is Gissing's greatest achievement in this novel — he makes us wince at Reardon and with him, simultaneously, and refuses to let either feeling win.
That unresolved sympathy — that question of whether we wince at Reardon or with him — is exactly where we need to go next.

Because the novel doesn't let us stay comfortable for long — and in our next segment, we'll follow Reardon himself into the full arc of his unravelling: the ambition, the despair, and the terrible logic of a talent breaking under pressure.
We've been talking about the machinery of Grub Street — the editors, the markets, the relentless pressure to produce.
Now I want to get to the man caught inside that machinery — Edwin Reardon, and what the novel does to him.
Oliver, you flagged something in your prep that I've been thinking about ever since.
You said Reardon's unravelling is vocal before it's anything else.
There's that moment in chapter seventeen where Amy's accent shifts, and Reardon hears her sounding like a woman arguing at a street corner.
Can you actually read that passage for us, and tell us what you're hearing in it?
Yes — and I want to read it, because reading it is the only way to show you what Gissing is doing.
He gives us two sentences and they contain an entire worldview collapsing.
Here it is, exactly as Gissing wrote it:
"With just such accent he had heard a wrangling woman retort upon her husband at the street corner. Is there then no essential difference between a woman of this world and one of that?"
That exclamation before it — 'Great Heaven!' — tells you everything about the pitch of his horror.
Reardon is not hearing Amy argue. He is hearing a class boundary dissolve.
And Gissing puts it as a question — 'Is there then no essential difference?' — because he genuinely doesn't answer it.
That open wound at the end of the sentence is what makes it theatrical. You can't close it neatly when you say it aloud.
Oliver, I'd push back, though — gently — on what you just called a 'class boundary dissolving.'
Because the boundary doesn't dissolve. It was always an illusion.
Amy hasn't become that street-corner woman. She's simply been stripped of the material conditions that made her seem different from her.
The most revealing thing in that passage is Reardon's horror itself — the word 'wrangling,' that involuntary recoil.
That is not a sensitive man perceiving a tragedy. That is class anxiety performing itself as aesthetic disgust.
Gissing is showing us Reardon's ideology, not endorsing it.
I'm afraid I find that reading rather too convenient, Daniel.
What Reardon is asking — 'Is there then no essential difference?' — is a genuinely philosophical question.
It is a question about whether character is formed by circumstance or whether it exists prior to circumstance.
You call his horror 'class anxiety.' I would call it something older — a terror at the fragility of what we mean by a person.
That is not ideology. That is a man discovering that the woman he loved may not be who he thought she was — or who she thought she was.
Edmund is onto something I don't want to let go of too quickly — and that is the physical dimension of the novel's tragedy.
Gissing doesn't just tell us Reardon is failing. He makes us see it in the body.
There's this devastating account in chapter fifteen — the prose is almost clinical in its cruelty:
"at thirty-three he would generally have been taken for forty."
Six words. And the arithmetic of it is more brutal than any adjective he could have chosen.
He goes on — the stoop, the stick, the hesitation in choosing words — the voice 'fallen to a lower key.'
That is a man being erased. And Gissing describes it with the detachment of a coroner.
Edmund, I want to bring you in here, because I think you'd want to defend Reardon against both Oliver and Daniel — in rather different ways.
You've got that passage from chapter four — Reardon talking about shrinking from conscious insincerity of workmanship.
You read that as the moral heart of the novel. But Daniel would say that conscience is a luxury a poor man can't afford.
Is Reardon's artistic integrity genuinely admirable — or is it, as Daniel would have it, a kind of slow suicide dressed up as principle?
It is admirable. Unreservedly so. And I won't be argued out of that.
Reardon says something here that I regard as one of the most honest sentences in the novel.
"There's the shrinking from conscious insincerity of workmanship — which most of the writers nowadays seem never to feel."
'It's good enough for the market' — Gissing follows immediately with that phrase, and the contrast is devastating.
Reardon knows the market exists. He knows what it wants. He simply cannot bring himself to give it less than his best.
To call that suicide is to say that integrity without a market is worthless. Which may be Daniel's view — but it is not Gissing's.
I'd say it very nearly is Gissing's view — and that's what makes the novel so uncomfortable.
The novel doesn't reward integrity. It watches integrity get ground down with a kind of pitiless accuracy.
And what's most remarkable is that Reardon himself sees the mechanism clearly — and still can't escape it.
There's the speech in chapter fifteen — Reardon speaking to Amy — that I think is the clearest-eyed passage in the entire novel.

"The world has no pity on a man who can't do or produce something it thinks worth money. You may be a divine poet, and if some good fellow doesn't take pity on you you will starve by the roadside. Society is as blind and brutal as fate."
That is not self-pity. That is accurate structural diagnosis.
And then — immediately — he says: 'I have no right to complain of my own ill-fortune; it's my own fault.'
He sees the system perfectly and then internalises the blame anyway. That is what ideology does to a person.
But Daniel, a weakened man says things a stronger man would not say. That is not lucid diagnosis — that is the voice of defeat.
There's something earlier in the novel — chapter six — where Reardon diagnoses himself with far greater precision.
"A temperament like mine can't pass through such a violent change of conditions without being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I left England."
He continues — and this is the crucial part — 'Intellectually, I have fallen back. But the due course of things is troubled by my poverty.'
He separates the intellectual from the economic. He believes recovery is possible if only the poverty could be lifted.
That is not a man without agency. That is a man whose agency has been systematically denied him — which is a rather different thing.
Oliver, there's a sentence in chapter twelve that you wanted to quote — and I think it might be the most devastating line in everything we've read today.
It's about how their relationship 'would not bear spoken comment' — both of them knowing it, neither saying it.
You read that silence as the most terrible thing in the novel. Daniel reads the same sentence as economic machinery. What do you hear when you say it?
Right. Here it is. And I want to read the full sentence because the syntax is doing as much work as the content:
"Their relations to each other — not long ago an inexhaustible topic — would not bear spoken comment; both were too conscious of the danger-signal when they looked that way."
'Not long ago an inexhaustible topic.' That parenthesis — the em-dash pair — is grief in grammatical form.
Once they talked endlessly about being together. Now they can't mention it at all. And the word 'danger-signal' — that's the giveaway.
It means: if we name what's happening, we can never un-name it. So both of them agree, silently, not to look.
That is not economic machinery. That is two people in a room, each pretending not to see the other drowning.
Oliver, I hear that — I really do — but the sentence before it is the one that matters to me.
Gissing writes that they've shifted from their old subjects 'to those mean concerns of material life which formerly they had agreed to dismiss as quickly as possible.'
The silence isn't purely emotional collapse. It is what poverty produces when it moves into a marriage.
And the novel is even cleaner about it later — chapter sixteen — where Reardon says simply:
"It seems to me, Amy, that your one desire is to get away from me, on whatever terms."
'On whatever terms.' That phrase contains the entire economics of the marriage in dissolution. He's not just losing her — he's watching her calculate the exit.
And yet — that line is Reardon speaking, not Gissing. We should be careful not to take Reardon's accusations as the novel's verdict on Amy.
The novel's portrait of their marriage is genuinely tragic precisely because neither of them is simply wrong.

Reardon says she wants to escape him. But Gissing also shows us — in that same chapter twelve passage — that Reardon himself has grown cold, has adopted a manner that 'was far from representing the truth.'
He condemns himself and feels wronged simultaneously. That is not ideological confusion. That is human nature, precisely observed.
Daniel, I want to push you to the hardest version of your argument, because I think you've been letting Reardon off the hook a little.
You said earlier that the cruelest thing Gissing does is let Reardon diagnose the system perfectly — and then watch him accept the blame anyway.
Edmund calls that spiritual capitulation. You'd call it something else.
But here's my question: is there anything Reardon could have done differently? Or does this novel foreclose that entirely?
The honest answer is: probably not. Not within the novel's logic.
And Gissing shows us why with devastating precision in that same chapter fifteen speech.
The phrase is: 'it's hard that I must be kicked aside as worthless just because I don't know a trade.'
The market doesn't recognize literary genius as a skill. It recognizes productivity — quantity, regularity, marketability.
Reardon has none of those things by temperament. And temperament, in this novel, is not something you overcome by virtue.
Edmund wants to call this tragedy. I'd call it a system working exactly as designed — and Reardon is the proof of concept.
I think you're both right and both slightly missing the point — because the novel also asks us to enjoy Reardon, which is a different demand entirely.
There is genuine pleasure in reading him — a great, doomed, self-aware, helpless man. Gissing writes him with relish.
That passage from chapter fifteen — 'no spring in his step,' 'voice fallen to a lower key,' 'wandering, sometimes a wild, expression to his eyes' — that is virtuoso writing.
The writer who composed that sentence is not merely diagnosing a system or charting a moral failure.
He is making something beautiful out of destruction. That is what novelists do with their best material — and Reardon is clearly his best material.
I think that's where we have to leave Reardon for now — caught between diagnosis and tragedy, between the system's logic and the novelist's art.
In the next part, we turn to the man who seems to have solved the problem Reardon couldn't — Jasper Milvain, who treats the market not as an enemy but as a game to be won.
We've been sitting with Reardon's particular kind of suffering — the man who can't bend.
Now I want to turn to the man who can — and does — with enormous relish.
Daniel, you said in our conversation before we recorded that Jasper Milvain isn't a cautionary tale — he's the system working exactly as designed.
But the man sits there and tells you to your face he'll never write anything of value and despises everyone who reads him.
At what point does rational self-preservation just become... being a bastard?
The framing of 'bastard' is interesting because it places the moral weight entirely on Jasper's shoulders — which is precisely what the novel refuses to do.
Gissing is describing a market that has restructured what it means to write for a living.
Jasper doesn't invent this logic — he simply reads it more clearly than anyone else in the novel.
Look at what he actually says to his sisters in chapter one.
"Literature nowadays is a trade. Putting aside men of genius, who may succeed by mere cosmic force, your successful man of letters is your skilful tradesman."
That is not a confession of vice — that is a market analysis.
And the horror is that he's correct.
I want to grant Daniel his structural reading — up to a point.
Yes, the literary market of 1882 is what it is. Gissing knows it intimately.
But Jasper is not a leaf blown by the market's wind. He is a man making choices.
He tells us so himself, with what I can only call a kind of appalling lucidity.
"I shall never write for writing's sake, only to make money. All my plans and efforts will have money in view — all."
That final 'all' is not the market speaking. That is a will.
And a will that has chosen its object with complete awareness is a moral fact, whatever the surrounding conditions.
Edmund always lands beautifully on the individual and then stops there.
But if the conditions of literary production systematically reward exactly what Jasper offers — speed, servility, the willingness to praise pompous idiocy — then calling it a 'will' explains nothing.
The book from chapter fourteen — Billington's 'Vagaries' — Jasper writes it up because the man lives in a big house and gives dinners.
And he says it without a flicker of shame:
"It's the easiest thing in the world to write laudation; only an inexperienced grumbler would declare it was easier to find fault."
The shame has been structurally eliminated. That's the point.
Oliver, you've been holding something back — I can see it.
You want to read Jasper as Gissing's great comic creation — almost affectionate.
There's a passage in chapter six — the 'my intuition is so strong' speech. Can you take us through it?
With the greatest of pleasure. Because this is where Gissing the entertainer — and I insist on that word — completely outruns Gissing the social anatomist.
Jasper is showing off here, and Gissing knows it, and we're meant to enjoy the performance.
He opens with a Falstaff quotation, for pity's sake — ''Tis my vocation, Hal!' — and then delivers this:
"My intuition is so strong that I can make a little experience go an immense way."
And then — and this is the stroke — he doesn't flinch from the confession at the heart of it.
"Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value; I shall always despise the people I write for. But my path will be that of success."
The man is an aria. You can't simply condemn an aria.
Oliver makes it irresistible, of course. He always does.
But I think the delight we take in the performance is precisely what Gissing is staging for us — and staging as a warning.
'Never in my life shall I do anything of solid literary value' — Jasper says this as a boast.
He doesn't say it with regret. He doesn't say it with irony. He says it as a settled fact about himself — cheerfully.
Now: self-knowledge without self-correction is not philosophy. It is not honesty. It is damnation with the lights on.
Edmund, I love 'damnation with the lights on' — I'm going to steal that.
But I'd push back on the idea that Gissing's structure is punishing Jasper.
Gissing the moralist tries to condemn him. Gissing the writer is charmed. And in any contest between those two, the writer wins.
Both of you are treating this as a question of aesthetics — charm versus damnation — and I want to pull it back to the page.
'I shall always despise the people I write for.' Think about what that means as a description of alienated labour.
Jasper is completely severed from any relationship with his audience, his product, his own capacity.
That's not a personality trait. That's what the market produces when it colonises literary life entirely.
Daniel, I want to press you on that — because the question of agency comes into sharp focus in chapter four, with Amy.
You've argued that her capitulation — 'art must be practised as a trade' — is coercion dressed up as common sense.
But isn't there a version where it's both? Where it is coercion AND she still chooses it?
Yes — and I want to be honest about that, because I think it's where the novel does its most uncomfortable work.
What Amy says is not false. Let me read it as it actually stands:

"Art must be practised as a trade, at all events in our time. This is the age of trade. Of course if one refuses to be of one's time, and yet hasn't the means to live independently, what can result but breakdown and wretchedness?"
That is a structurally accurate description of the situation. She is not wrong.
But there is something chilling in the ease with which she internalises it — and then invokes Milvain as her authority.
The coercion and the choice arrive together, inseparably. And that is not a comfort — that is the trap.
I find myself in unexpected agreement with Daniel on the facts of the passage, if not the framing.
Amy is not a fool. She sees clearly. And that is precisely what makes her choice — for it is a choice — so troubling.
Where Daniel says 'the market produces this,' I say: the market offers the temptation, and a person accepts it.
The distinction matters enormously — because if agency is entirely dissolved into structure, then no one is responsible for anything, and literature stops being about human beings.
What strikes me about Amy's speech is the rhythm of it — 'This is the age of trade' — said as if it closes the argument.
She's not agonising. She's not performing reluctance. She's quoting Milvain back at her husband as if it were scripture.
And Gissing gives her no great scene of inner conflict before she says it. She's just... arrived there.
Oliver, final question — and I want all three of you on this.
You said the novel's real horror is that Jasper succeeds by telling the truth about how the world works.
He ends up with the career, with Marian, with everything. Does Gissing mean us to find that satisfying? Is there any consolation in this book at all?
The consolation, if there is one, is purely aesthetic — which is to say, it's the novel itself.
Gissing writes with such precision about the machinery of failure that the writing becomes a kind of redemption for what it describes.
Jasper wins. But the man who made Jasper so vivid, so quotable, so brilliantly candid — he was not Jasper.
I would say the consolation lies in the form of the novel — which is itself an act of the imagination Jasper has entirely foreclosed.
He has chosen success. Gissing has chosen truth. And truth, in literature, outlasts success.
I think the novel refuses consolation — deliberately, rigorously, as a formal choice.
Jasper's victory is the system demonstrating that it works. And the novel shows us that at length, without flinching.
To ask for consolation from a novel this honest is to ask it to lie to us.
Three completely different novels — and somehow all three of them are right.
We've been circling Jasper Milvain as the man who understands the market and rises through it.
But there's someone else in this novel whose labour feeds that same market — and who has far less freedom to choose her relationship to it.
Marian Yule, in the Reading Room of the British Museum, copying out other people's words for other people's books. We'll go there next.

segments.title: Marian's Bind: Labour and Longing in the Library

utterances.text: We've been talking about Jasper Milvain's calculated navigation of the literary market — a man who treats writing as commerce and sleeps soundly for it.
Now I want to turn to the character who stands as something like his moral opposite — Marian Yule, trapped in the British Museum, grinding away at work she despises.
Oliver, let me start with you — you described the 'valley of the shadow of books' line as both genuinely moving and slightly ridiculous.
Can you read it for us and say what you mean by that?
Right, well — the passage is very short, which is part of what makes it devastating.
Gissing gives us precisely two sentences, and the second one does everything.
Here it is:
"She could labour on in the valley of the shadow of books, for a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment strike into its musty gloom."
Now — 'the valley of the shadow of books.'
That is a man rewriting the Twenty-Third Psalm and replacing death with bibliography.
It's funny — it's supposed to be a little funny.
And then 'a ray of dazzling sunshine' — well, that's not ironic, that's genuinely tender.
Gissing is doing both things at once: the bathos and the ache.
The question I keep circling is whether he believes in that sunshine.
He doesn't.
Or rather — the novel doesn't allow him to, whatever he personally wished for Marian.
The sunshine is ideological sedation.
It's the story a woman in Marian's position must tell herself in order to keep labouring under conditions that would otherwise be unbearable.
The novel shows us that those conditions — the foggy Reading Room, the manufacture of copy, the father who extracts her labour — are structural, not circumstantial.
Hope, in that context, isn't heroic — it's what keeps the machine running.
I think that is a very eloquent way of reducing a young woman's capacity for love to a function of her economic position.
The sunshine isn't ideology — it is hope.
And what Gissing is doing, I think, is anatomising the conditions under which a particular kind of survival becomes possible.
That is not an indictment of Marian — it is an act of profound sympathy with her.
Gissing understood what it meant to keep one's spirits from collapse in circumstances of relentless drudgery.
He was not diagnosing false consciousness — he was writing, with full moral seriousness, about the cost of endurance.
Daniel, let me press you on something — because there's a line later in Chapter Eight that you've been particularly insistent about.
The 'mere machine' line — you said it isn't metaphor, it's diagnosis.
But Marian says it about herself, in her own head.
How do you square the character saying something with the novel meaning it?
The passage goes:
"She was not a woman, but a mere machine for reading and writing."
Now — it is in Marian's consciousness, yes.
But the novel does not contradict it.
The narration doesn't pull back and say 'poor Marian, she's being too hard on herself.'
The narration confirms it.
Her father does not think of this — the novel shows us that directly.
The question 'did her father never think of this?' is rhetorical, and the answer the novel gives is: he didn't.
Marian's self-description is the most accurate thing in the book — because she sees herself the way the system actually sees her.
That is precisely where I part company with Daniel.
'A mere machine for reading and writing' is a cry of the heart — not a thesis about the organisation of labour.
Marian is in her room, weeping.
She has just come back from Finden — from a glimpse of something she might have had.
The passage tells us: 'For a moment, in the lanes about Finden, there had come to her a vision of joy such as fate owed her youth; but it had faded.'
That is grief, not theory.
And I think Daniel's reading, for all its rigour, makes the same mistake her father makes — it refuses to see a person.
That is a very pointed comparison, and I'll accept it as a genuine challenge rather than a debating point.
But I'd say: the father refuses to see her because seeing her would cost him something.
I am insisting on the structural reading precisely because I don't want to aestheticise her suffering — to make it beautiful and leave the conditions that produced it untouched.
Can I say something that might annoy both of you?
I think Gissing is doing something subtler — he's giving Marian genuine intelligence, and then showing that intelligence to be, in the most heartbreaking way, useless.
There's a passage that Edmund is looking at — the one about her candour and clear-sightedness.

"Her candour was allied with clear insight into the possibilities of falsehood; she was not readily the victim of illusion; thinking much, and speaking little, she had not come to her twenty-third year without perceiving what a distance lay between a girl's dream of life as it might be and life as it is."
She sees everything clearly.
And it changes nothing.
That's the particular cruelty Gissing is working with — not ignorance as tragedy, but perception as impotence.
Edmund, that's almost exactly your claim about Marian — that her clarity is her nobility.
And yet Daniel reads that same quality as what makes her suffering more conscious without making her any more free.
Who's right about what Gissing actually thinks of her?
I'm not certain those positions are as opposed as they appear.
The passage ends — and this is the line that matters most to me — with the observation that, had Marian always spoken her thoughts, she would have earned a reputation for cynicism.
She doesn't.
She keeps her counsel.
That is a form of moral discipline — and I think Gissing regards it as such.
Her intelligence is her nobility, yes — and also, I would grant Daniel this, her undoing.
But that is tragedy in the classical sense — not a system's failure, but a character's greatness turned against itself by circumstance.
'Classical tragedy' is a very convenient frame — it dignifies the suffering and leaves the cause in the hands of the gods.
The cause here is not fate — it is her father's debt, the literary market, and the complete absence of any mechanism by which a woman of her ability could earn a living on her own terms.
Look at what she thinks in the Museum — Chapter Eight.
"What unspeakable folly! To write — was not that the joy and the privilege of one who had an urgent message for the world?"
She knows, for a moment, what writing should be.
And she is sitting in a fog, producing copy for a market that will consume it and forget it.
That gap — between what she knows and what she does — is not a failure of character.
It is what the system requires of her.
That passage in the Museum is extraordinary to perform.
Gissing sets the scene so precisely — 'a taste of fog grew perceptible in the warm, headachy air.'
'Headachy.' That word is doing so much — it's physical, it's comic, it's perfectly miserable.
And then Marian just — lets her hands fall.
She stops pretending.
That gesture — heedless of who's watching — is a tiny act of private revolt that goes absolutely nowhere.
And whether you call that a glimpse of radical consciousness or just a very perceptive young woman having a profoundly bad Thursday — I'm not sure Gissing would choose between those readings.
Oliver, you've said Marian sees the trap and still reaches toward love.
But Daniel would say she has no real options, and Edmund would say she's constitutionally incapable of the self-deception that might have saved her.
Does calling it 'paralysis' let Gissing off the hook for what actually happens to her?
That's the sharpest question you can ask of this novel, I think.
Because 'paralysis' can be a way of saying: look how terrible her situation is, isn't that moving — and then walking away.
Gissing is always in danger of that — of making the sadness so beautifully rendered that we find it pleasurable rather than disturbing.
The sunshine line again — 'a ray of dazzling sunshine might at any moment strike into its musty gloom' — that's gorgeous.
And I think Gissing knows it's gorgeous.
The writer in him is pleased with that sentence even as the moralist in him knows it will not save her.
I think that is actually the most generous account of what Gissing is doing — and the truest.
He does not let his characters off easily.
Marian's intelligence — her refusal to be 'readily the victim of illusion' — is real, it is admirable, and it costs her enormously.
Gissing is not off the hook, as you put it, because the novel earns its sorrow on the page.
What lets a novelist off the hook is sentimentality — prettifying what should wound.
This novel wounds.
I won't dissent from that — only to add that knowing something wounds is not the same as knowing why.
The novel shows us the wound with great precision.
It is less confident about the knife.
We've arrived at something rather dark — Marian seeing clearly, suffering precisely, and hope functioning as a kind of anaesthetic.
Which might be the right moment to ask how Gissing manages to make a novel this grim also — at moments — genuinely funny.
That's what we're turning to next — the comic register of New Grub Street, and why it might be inseparable from the tragedy.

segments.title: Wit and Gloom: Gissing's Comic Register

utterances.text: We've been sitting with Marian in that library — all that labour, all that longing, pressing down on a single human body.
Now I want to turn to the novel's other register entirely — because New Grub Street is also, in places, extraordinarily funny.
It is funny — and dangerously so, which is the whole problem.
Jasper Milvain gets the best arguments and the clearest prose in the novel.
When you read him aloud — and I have, many times — there's a point where you stop performing and start agreeing.
The host asked me in our chat about that line — about the genius of vulgarity — and I want to read it, because it matters how it sounds.
'To please the vulgar you must, one way or another, incarnate the genius of vulgarity.'
Now — is that Jasper's creed, or is it Gissing's aesthetic manifesto?
Because the sentence is too beautifully made to be merely satirised.
Oliver, I think you're being seduced — which is precisely Gissing's point.
Jasper isn't right because his prose is elegant. He's dangerous because it is.
What Gissing gives us is a man talking himself past his own conscience — sentence by polished sentence.
Listen to what comes just before that line — the spirit in which Jasper frames it all.
'Let us use our wits to earn money, and make the best we can of our lives.'
That 'let us' is the voice of a man recruiting accomplices, not confessing a philosophy.
To call that authorial complicity seems to me a category error — it is the portraiture of spiritual disease, not its celebration.
Edmund, I don't disagree that it's spiritual disease — I'm saying it's a very attractive disease, and Gissing knows it.
Earlier in the same scene Jasper is absolutely direct about the mechanics — methodical, almost cheerful.

'Writing is a business. Get together half-a-dozen fair specimens of the Sunday-school prize; study them; discover the essential points of such composition; hit upon new attractions; then go to work methodically, so many pages a day.'
That is a man who has found peace, Edmund. A terrible peace — but peace nonetheless.
And Gissing writes it with such relish that I genuinely cannot tell where the satirist ends and the convert begins.
I've been listening to you both circle around the most important word in those passages, which is 'mob.'
Jasper's comedy of self-justification is built on that foundation — the contempt for the market audience is structural, not incidental.
He says he will write for the upper-middle-class intelligentsia — 'people who can't distinguish between stones and paste.'
So the class calculus is explicit: Jasper knows exactly which layer of the market he's extracting value from.
Where I want to take us is away from Jasper entirely — because Jasper is the man who wins this game.
The evidence of what Jasper's logic actually costs is sitting at a desk in Chapter Twenty-Seven — a man named Sykes.
Daniel, read it to us. Because I think you're right that we've been avoiding it.
Gissing describes Sykes — shabby tweeds, a silk hat that has been, and I love this word, 'moulting' — and then he gives us this.

'With coat-sleeve turned back, so as to give free play to his right hand and wrist, revealing meanwhile a flannel shirt of singular colour, and with his collar unbuttoned — he wore no tie — to leave his throat at ease as he bent myopically over the paper, he was writing at express speed, evidently in the full rush of the ardour of composition.'
And then — 'The veins of his forehead were dilated, and his chin pushed forward in a way that made one think of a racing horse.'
That's not a joke. That's a body the market has turned into a machine.
Jasper talks about vulgarity as a game of skill. Sykes shows you what the game produces.
Edmund calls Jasper a spiritual failure. But Sykes isn't a spiritual failure — he's a casualty.
I won't dismiss Sykes — that description is one of the finest pieces of grotesque portraiture in the novel.
But Daniel, a casualty of what exactly?
The novel surrounds Sykes with men who make different choices — Biffen, even Reardon in his ruinous way, refuses the logic Jasper preaches.
Gissing is too honest to present the market as the only force in play.
Character matters in this novel — it always matters in great novels — and to efface it in favour of systemic forces is, I think, a kind of sentimentality in reverse.
I find myself wanting to defend both of you and that probably means Gissing has won.
Because that scene with Sykes is comic and tragic simultaneously — and it's comic because it's tragic.
A 'flannel shirt of singular colour' — Gissing will not tell you what the colour is. He makes you imagine it. That's the joke and the horror in one phrase.
And there's no contradiction between Daniel's reading and Edmund's, really.
Sykes might be a casualty of the system and a man whose character made him vulnerable to it. Gissing's genius is that he won't arbitrate.
Here's the question I want to put to all three of you. Is Jasper Milvain funny — and does it matter whether we're laughing with him or at him?
He is funny — wickedly funny — and I think Gissing intends us to feel the discomfort of that laughter.

When Jasper says — almost in the same breath — 'What the devil — I mean what on earth is there in typography to make everything it deals with sacred?' — that self-correction is brilliant comic timing.
He catches himself swearing in front of his sisters and pivots without losing a beat. It's charm. It's practised charm.
We laugh — and then we notice we've laughed — and that is where Gissing wants us.
With or at him — I'm not sure that distinction survives Jasper. He's already anticipated both positions.
He says he'll write for people 'who can't distinguish between stones and paste' — that includes us, the readers, if we're laughing at the wit without seeing what it costs.
The comedy is the trap. Jasper is most dangerous when he's most enjoyable.
I think those are both right, which is why I'd rather talk about Fadge for a moment.
Because The Current and its editorial philosophy is where Jasper's logic, taken to its conclusion, arrives. And Gissing describes it with magnificent nastiness.
The line that has lived in my head for twenty years is this one.
'To assail an author without increasing the number of his readers is the perfection of journalistic skill.'
Gissing calls it 'the perfection of journalistic skill.' That is a sentence that knows exactly what it is doing.
He performs the sin he's diagnosing — the sentence is a piece of flippant brilliance about flippant brilliance.
That I would frame differently. It is not Gissing performing the sin — it is Gissing exhibiting wickedness stated as axiom.
There's a moral distance in that sentence — 'the perfection of' — it is a verdict, not a celebration.
Dr Johnson remarked that the road to hell is paved with good intentions. Gissing's road is paved with good sentences — and he knows it.
It's capitalism's operating manual — and it's funny precisely because capitalism's logic, stated plainly, always sounds like satire.
Gissing doesn't need to add irony. The system is already absurd when you write it down with sufficient clarity.
That's why the comedy in this novel is so unsettling — you can't always find the ironic frame. Sometimes it's just the plain fact.
And that, I think, is why the comedy never quite lets you go. It keeps sliding between pleasure and accusation.
Which brings us — very naturally, I think — to the question of how Gissing actually constructs this effect at the level of the prose itself.
The form of New Grub Street — how it's shaped, how time moves in it, what the structure is doing — is our next question.

segments.title: Form and Decay: How Gissing Tells New Grub Street

utterances.text: We've been talking about Gissing's comic register — the dark wit that sits just beneath the surface of even his most painful scenes.
But comedy, of course, is inseparable from form — from the way a writer chooses to arrange experience on the page.
Oliver, I want to start with something you said to me before we recorded — that Biffen's cold-in-the-head speech is actually funny.
Most readers encounter that passage and take it completely straight — as Gissing's own artistic manifesto.
Can you read it for us and make the case?
Delighted to — because this is the passage that made me laugh out loud the first time I read it, and I want to pin down exactly why.
Biffen is delivering this with absolute earnestness, remember — there is not a flicker of irony in the man.
He says — and here it is:
"When the man and woman are to meet for a great scene of passion, let it all be frustrated by one or other of them having a bad cold in the head."
And then — this is my favourite bit — he goes on: "Let the pretty girl get a disfiguring pimple on her nose just before the ball."
Now, Gissing writes this with a completely straight face, and that's what makes it so delicious.
Biffen is performing the death of romanticism — with all the solemnity of a high priest conducting a funeral.
If Biffen were Gissing's simple mouthpiece, the novel would be intolerable — a pamphlet with drains.
I find that reading slightly too comfortable, I'm afraid.
Biffen is comic, yes — but Gissing is also, I think, genuinely interested in what Biffen is saying.
The cold-in-the-head is absurd in its specificity, but the principle behind it is quite serious.
Look at what Biffen says just before that — the programme he lays out in the earlier passage is genuinely arresting.
"I want to deal with the essentially unheroic, with the day-to-day life of that vast majority of people who are at the mercy of paltry circumstance."
That is not a joke.
That is a genuine artistic credo — flawed in its execution, perhaps, but not absurd in its aspiration.
I'd say you're both partly right, but neither of you has said the most important thing yet.
Biffen isn't just an aesthetic theorist — he's a man trying to see his own class with unclouded eyes.
When he says 'the ignobly decent,' he's naming something real — the working poor who are neither tragic heroes nor comic grotesques but simply ground down.
And Oliver's right that there's comedy — but the comedy is politically loaded.
We laugh at the cold in the head, and then we catch ourselves laughing, and we feel the discomfort of that.
Because what Biffen is describing is what these people's lives actually look like — and we've been trained by fiction to find that grotesque.
That's very good — the guilt-mechanism reading — and I don't entirely resist it.
But notice what Gissing actually does with the novel he's writing while Biffen is pronouncing all this.
New Grub Street is not 'Mr. Bailey, Grocer' — it's far more dramatically orchestrated than anything Biffen describes.
There are great scenes of passion — there is melodrama, there is a death, there is a marriage destroyed.
So the novel itself is a kind of revenge against its characters' theories — Gissing simply cannot help being a better storyteller than his own doctrine allows.
Edmund, I want to pull you into something quite specific — the chapter 31 passage, where the narrator steps forward and defends Reardon and Biffen directly.
All three of you want to quote it, which tells me it's doing something different for each of you.
What does it actually say to you when you read it?
It says something that I think is deeply conservative — in the best sense of that word.
The narrator steps outside the story and speaks with real moral authority — not polemical anger, but settled conviction.
The sentence that arrests me is this:
"These two were richly endowed with the kindly and the imaginative virtues; if fate threw them amid incongruous circumstances, is their endowment of less value?"
That is not a socialist argument — it is a Burkean one.
The value of Reardon and Biffen is prior to the market — it precedes any economic assessment.
Gissing is insisting that there are human virtues which economic life simply has no capacity to measure — and that the fault lies in the narrowness of the measure, not the deficiency of the men.
Edmund and I will rarely agree, but on the import of that passage I think we're closer than he realises.
Where we part company is on the mechanism.
Edmund says the fault lies in the narrowness of the measure — I say: who built that measuring apparatus, and in whose interests does it operate?
The narrator calls their passivity 'their nature and their merit' — but Gissing is also showing us a publishing market that has no mechanism for rewarding that particular nature.
The 'humane order of Society' that Gissing invokes — the one that would value these men — is conspicuously absent.
That absence is the indictment.
I love watching you two reach almost the same conclusion from completely opposite directions.
But I want to say something about the prose itself — because the narrator's voice in that passage is doing something formally unusual.
He addresses the reader directly — 'You scorn their passivity' — and that second-person turn is a rhetorical challenge.
It implicates us — the readers of literary novels, the people likely to pick up New Grub Street in the first place — as precisely the 'average man' whose coarse demands have destroyed these two.
Daniel, let me push you further into the disagreement — the chapter 5 passage about Reardon and what he needs to write.
Edmund reads it as a character portrait — a man who understands his own limits.
You read it as something else entirely, I think.
Who's right about what Gissing is actually doing there?
The passage does something very cunning, and I think Edmund is half reading it correctly.
Gissing gives us this sentence:
"He was the kind of man who cannot struggle against adverse conditions, but whom prosperity warms to the exercise of his powers."
Now Edmund will say: this is a character flaw, a temperament — and there's no doubt Gissing intends us to see Reardon clearly.
But look at what prosperity actually means here — it means having a legacy, having capital, not being under the cosh of the monthly deadline.
The market doesn't produce the conditions in which Reardon can work — and then the market condemns him for failing to work.
That's not individual weakness — that's a structural trap with individual faces.
I anticipated Daniel would say exactly that — and I respect the argument, even as I find it finally evasive.
Gissing describes Reardon's need for ease with the precision of a physician — 'his delicate mental organism,' 'fatal to the peculiar merit of his work.'
This is not a description of economic victimhood — it is a portrait of a man who knows himself, and who makes certain choices accordingly.
Reardon's tragedy is partly that he lacks the will — as well as the resources — to protect what he knows he needs.
The system is brutal, yes — but Daniel's reading risks exonerating the will entirely, which Gissing does not do.
Oliver — I want to give you the last word on the biggest question in this segment.
There's that passage in chapter 31 where Reardon says — and this is extraordinary prose — that he has already died.
You said it has a liturgical quality — almost Hamlet.
So: is Gissing arguing that form itself — the writer's shaping hand — is the only thing that can redeem unglamorous suffering? And if so, what does that mean for Biffen's whole project?
Right — so let me read it, because it has to be heard.
"To have had even a small reputation, and to have outlived it, is a sort of anticipation of death.
The man Edwin Reardon, whose name was sometimes spoken in a tone of interest, is really and actually dead.
And what remains of me is resigned to that.
I have an odd fancy that it will make death itself easier; it is as if only half of me had now to die."
'Only half of me had now to die' — I defy anyone to tell me that's ignobly decent prose.
That is shaped, musical, deliberate — it's Gissing giving Reardon a death-speech worthy of the stage.
And that's my answer to the Biffen question — the novel structurally defeats its own realist characters, because Gissing cannot resist the shaping hand.
The suffering needs form to be bearable — and the form is a kind of argument that Biffen can never make.
I want to push back on one word — 'bearable.'
Oliver's reading aestheticises the suffering — makes it consoling.
But Reardon is not just a doomed romantic — he is a man killed by a specific market at a specific historical moment.
The beauty of that prose is real — but it is also, in a way, the thing that lets us off the hook.
We weep, we admire the sentences, and we don't ask: what kind of literary economy produces this casualty?
And there I think Daniel has — for once — said something I find genuinely moving.
Because Gissing is doing both things at once.
The form elevates — and the elevation is a kind of accusation.
He is saying: look at what this man was capable of feeling — and look at what the world made of him.
'Look at what the world made of him' — I think that may be the sentence this whole segment has been building toward.
Form, ambition, the cost of making art in a market that doesn't want what you have to offer — these questions sit at the very heart of New Grub Street.

In our final segment, we'll ask what the novel as a whole says about ambition — not just artistic ambition, but the will to survive and to prevail in an industrial culture that measures everything in column-inches and circulations.

segments.title: Closing: The Cost of Ambition in Industrial Culture

utterances.text: We've been talking about how Gissing shapes the novel's form to enact its argument — the prose itself performing exhaustion.
Now I want to come at the same question from the other direction: not how the novel is made, but what it costs — the human cost of ambition in a literary culture built on compromise.
Oliver, I want to start with you — and I want to ask you to do something.
You told me before we came on that you'd want to read the fog passage — c30:p150 — almost liturgically, like a funeral rite.
So before Daniel tells us it's a crime scene and Edmund tells us it's a study in moral collapse — would you just read it for us?
And then tell us why the sound of it matters.
I'm very glad you asked, because this passage should be heard before it's argued over.
Gissing gives us something here that is almost unprecedented in Victorian prose — a physical atmosphere that doesn't symbolize suffering, it literally delivers it.
Listen to what he writes:
"The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be smelt and tasted."
"Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul."
That phrase — 'the very reek of the bottomless pit' — is Dantean, and it's meant to be.
But notice what Gissing does with the sound before he gets there: 'smelt and tasted' — those short, hard monosyllables — the prose is making you breathe the fog.
When you perform this aloud, you slow almost to a stop at 'bottomless pit' — not for effect, but because the sentence has no more air in it.
That reading was extraordinary, and I mean that without reservation.
But I want to push back on the word 'Dantean' — or rather, I want to ask what it costs us to reach for Dante here.
Because the fog is not metaphysical. The fog is London in 1891.

It is the product of coal burned by a particular economic system — and Marian is lying in it because that same system has destroyed her prospects, stolen her inheritance, and ground her father down to a bitter husk.
When Gissing writes 'poisoning the soul,' I agree it's beautiful — but the beauty is doing something specific.
It makes the class exhaustion visible on a body — Marian's body — in a way that statistics or polemic never could.
So does the beauty get in the way? No. The beauty is the argument — delivered through the nervous system rather than the intellect.
I find myself in the unusual position of agreeing with Daniel and Oliver simultaneously — which ought to alarm us all.
What strikes me about that passage is that the fog's moral weight depends entirely on our prior knowledge of Marian as a character of genuine integrity.
If she were a lesser soul — if she had Jasper's flexibility, shall we say — the fog would be merely unpleasant.
It is precisely because she cannot accommodate herself to the world that the world becomes, for her, infernal.
That is not a structural argument. That is a moral one.
Which brings us to Jasper — because if Marian is the person who can't accommodate herself, Jasper is the one who has made accommodation into an art form.
Edmund, you've said something that surprised me — that Jasper's most famous line is actually a moment of genuine self-knowledge, almost dignified.

I know Daniel and Oliver want that line too, and they'll mean something entirely different by it. So let's hear your reading first — is Jasper being honest, or performing honesty to get away with something?
The passage is in Chapter 24, and it deserves to be heard precisely.
"Nearly all men who have their way to make think as I do, but most feel obliged to adopt a false tone, to talk about literary conscientiousness, and so on."
"I simply say what I think, with no pretences. I should like to be conscientious, but it's a luxury I can't afford."
Now. What I hear in that is not cynicism — or not only cynicism.
I hear a man who has looked at himself without flinching and named what he is.
That is rarer than we like to admit. Most men in Jasper's position would dress it up in the language of vocation. He does not.
Whether that honesty redeems him is another matter entirely — I rather think it doesn't — but it is, at minimum, a form of moral seriousness.
Edmund, I want to name the disagreement directly, because I think it's the sharpest one in this novel.
You're framing Jasper's transparency as individual moral courage. I think his transparency is itself a form of institutional power.
When Jasper says 'nearly all men who have their way to make think as I do' — he's not confessing. He's recruiting.
He's normalising a particular relationship to the literary market — one in which conscience is always deferred, always unaffordable.
The system doesn't need Jasper to be corrupt. It needs him to be cheerfully, openly, *helpfully* corrupt — so that everyone around him adjusts their expectations downward.
His honesty is the most useful thing about him. And that's not dignity — that's function.
I think you're both right, and that is exactly why the passage is so uncomfortable to perform.
When I read that line — 'I should like to be conscientious, but it's a luxury I can't afford' — there is a tiny, almost imperceptible hesitation in Jasper before 'luxury.'
Or there should be. A trained actor finds it.
Because in that gap — between 'should like' and 'can't afford' — is the whole tragedy of New Grub Street.
Jasper knows what he's given up. The system doesn't care.
And that gap, as Oliver calls it, is where Marian lives — at the other end of the same system.
Daniel, Oliver told me before we started that he thinks Marian's outburst in Chapter 21 — the 'poisons men's minds' speech — has hysteria in it alongside the moral clarity.
That she's exhausted and desperate, not simply right. Does that reading let the profession off the hook — or does it actually strengthen your argument?
Marian's line is devastating precisely because it arrives at the moment of maximum pressure.
She says to her father:
"Literary quarrels have made you incapable of judging honestly in things such as this. I wish I could have done for ever with the hateful profession that so poisons men's minds."
Oliver says there's hysteria in that. And yes — she is exhausted, she is desperate.
But what the system does — what it always does — is produce exactly that kind of fracture in people.
It breaks down the capacity for measured response, for calm judgment, for the dignified moral reasoning Edmund admires.
So when Oliver says she's hysterical, he's right — and that hysteria is the system's signature on her body. It doesn't let the profession off the hook; it writes the indictment more clearly.
I don't retreat from that word — hysteria — but I want to be precise about what I mean by it.
Marian is right. The profession does poison men's minds — her father is the proof standing in front of her.
But the speech also arrives out of grief for what she has lost — not just an argument she has won.
When you perform it, you have to hold both registers at once: the clarity of someone who finally sees the truth, and the pain of someone who would give anything not to have seen it.
Gissing doesn't let her be simply heroic. She's right and she's broken. That's the harder thing to play.
Oliver has put it well, and I find I can accept Daniel's formulation too — up to a point.
The fracture Daniel describes is real. But I would note that Marian's fracture is also the mark of her seriousness.
A woman of Jasper's temperament would not be broken by this — she would accommodate, and survive, and be diminished in a way that left no visible scar.
The suffering is inseparable from the integrity. Gissing understood that, I think, more deeply than he sometimes gets credit for.
Let me put a final question to all three of you, and I want to ask it of Edmund first, because it's the one he'll find hardest to agree with.
Edmund, you've said Gissing is asking us to witness betrayal, not to reform the world. Daniel thinks the ending proves the system is working exactly as designed — no escape.
Oliver thinks you have to perform it with absolute seriousness, no irony at all. Are any of those three positions actually in conflict — or are they, at some level, the same argument?
I confess I have been bracing for that question since we began.
Here is what I think: tragedy and indictment are not opposites. They are the same event perceived from different distances.
At close range — Oliver's range, the performer's range — you see individual souls destroyed. That demands absolute seriousness.
From Daniel's distance, you see the mechanism that destroyed them. That demands the same seriousness, expressed differently.
What I resist is the implication that witnessing tragedy and seeking structural change are somehow incompatible.
The novel holds both. That is precisely why we are still arguing about it a hundred and thirty years later.
I'll take Edmund's olive branch, though I'll note he's smuggled something past us in the word 'distance.'
Because the structural view isn't a matter of standing further back — it's a matter of asking who built the room.

What makes this novel genuinely radical is that Gissing shows us, with almost clinical precision, that the people who succeed — Jasper — and the people who are destroyed — Marian, Reardon — are produced by identical pressures.
The fog poisons Marian's soul. The market poisons Jasper's — except he's learned to call the poison 'realism' and live on it.
And that is why you cannot play the ending with irony.
Because irony implies a safe position from which you observe. Gissing gives us no such position.
Edmund is right that it's tragedy. Daniel is right that it's indictment. Both require you to mean every word.
The fog. The luxury Jasper can't afford. The hateful profession that poisons men's minds.
Gissing earned all three of those phrases. The least we can do is deliver them as though we mean them too.
I think that's as good a place to end as any — and a better one than most.
We've moved today from the fog over Marian's pillow to the market logic in Jasper's mouth — and all three of you have shown why this novel refuses to let either argument win cleanly.

My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, whose reading of that fog passage I won't easily forget; to Sir Edmund Leigh, who kept moral seriousness in the room even when the argument pulled against it; and to Daniel Rosen, who reminded us that the reek of the bottomless pit has an address and a postcode.
And to our listeners — thank you for staying with us through New Grub Street.
It is a novel that asks an uncomfortable question of anyone who makes things for money — and that, one suspects, is most of us.
We hope it's given you something to carry away.

c27:p105.text:
‘With what magnificent scorn they would turn from us and our squalid
      feast! They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school
      men, University men, club men, society men. An income of less than three
      or four hundred a year is inconceivable to them; that seems the minimum
      for an educated man’s support. It would be small-minded to think of them
      with rancour, but, by Apollo! I know that we should change places with
      them if the work we have done were justly weighed against theirs.’
c27:p105.summary: Reardon condemns the successful novelists as public-school men incapable of understanding poverty; he insists their literary work is inferior to his own but serves the market demand, and asserts that if true merit were weighed, he and Biffen would triumph.
c27:p105.best_quote: They have never known struggle; not they. They are public-school men, University men, club men, society men.

c27:p121.text:
They repaired to the haunt in question. A flight of stairs brought them to
      a small room in which were exposed the daily newspapers; another ascent,
      and they were in a room devoted to magazines, chess, and refreshments; yet
      another, and they reached the department of weekly publications; lastly,
      at the top of the house, they found a lavatory, and a chamber for the use
      of those who desired to write. The walls of this last retreat were of blue
      plaster and sloped inwards from the floor; along them stood school desks
      with benches, and in one place was suspended a ragged and dirty card
      announcing that paper and envelopes could be purchased downstairs. An
      enormous basket full of waste-paper, and a small stove, occupied two
      corners; ink blotches, satirical designs, and much scribbling in pen and
      pencil served for mural adornment. From the adjacent lavatory came sounds
      of splashing and spluttering, and the busy street far below sent up its
      confused noises.
c27:p121.summary: Gissing provides a detailed topography of the penny reading-room: successive floors with newspapers, magazines, chess, and finally a writing-room with sloped blue walls, school desks, a trash basket, a small stove, and walls decorated with scribbling and ink blotches.
c27:p121.best_quote: The walls of this last retreat were of blue plaster and sloped inwards from the floor; along them stood school desks with benches, and in one place was suspended a ragged and dirty card announcing that paper and envelopes could be purchased downstairs.

Could Amy’s voice sound like that? Great Heaven! With just such accent he
      had heard a wrangling woman retort upon her husband at the street corner.
      Is there then no essential difference between a woman of this world and
      one of that? Does the same nature lie beneath such unlike surfaces?
c17:p87.summary: Reardon realizes Amy's voice and manner now resemble a lower-class quarreling woman, and he wonders if character is determined entirely by circumstance.
